title: Long-term observation of IBD patients - a nationwide German IBD Registry "CEDUR"
summary:
In Germany, approximately 600,000 patients suffer from inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). Exact data on the prevalence of these diseases are not yet available. However, studies show that the frequency and incidence of IBD are increasing over time and in different regions worldwide.

In principle, inflammatory bowel diseases can be very well treated according to disease activity and course with the currently available medications. Over the past years, new, innovative, and highly effective therapies (biologics and small molecules) have been introduced into clinical care. However, these new treatment options require highly specialized medical expertise and a significant amount of time for patient management.

Recent data indicate that younger patient groups, especially those in the early stages of disease or in mid-working life, are still being treated suboptimally. On average, it still takes around two years from the onset of first symptoms to a correct diagnosis. During this period, irreversible damage to the gastrointestinal tract may already occur.

Despite convincing scientific evidence, a considerable proportion of patients are still treated over long periods with corticosteroids and mesalazine, while the use of immunosuppressants and biologics remains rare.

Through early and consistent implementation of current treatment guidelines, patients could achieve a high level of well-being, and potential long-term complications could be avoided. Moreover, unnecessary costs for therapy, hospitalization, and surgery could be reduced. The number of sick leaves and early retirements would also decrease, resulting in a significant economic relief for society.

To achieve this goal, it is essential to establish and document standardized and practical care pathways that enable improved patient management.

Against this background, the first independent national IBD registry “CEDUR” (Chronisch Entzündliche Darmerkrankungen – ein Unabhängiges Register) was established.
This registry aims to contribute to improved healthcare research in Germany through a methodically structured collection of data on therapeutic effects, real-world treatment patterns, therapy costs, pharmacoeconomic aspects, and the prevalence of IBD — with the ultimate goal of improving healthcare quality in the long term.
conditions: Crohn's disease and Ulcerative Colitis and indeterminate Colitis

interventions.name: Observational study in adult patients with IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease). Observation period: 10 years and more. Data collected includes quality of life (PROM-10, sIBDQ, Facit-F, bowel urgency), pharmacoeconomic data (hospitalization, sick days), smoking and eating habits, disease classification

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Crohn's disease, Ulcerative Colitis or Indeterminate Colitis
Exclusion criteria:
Gastrointestinal disorders other than those mentioned above
